clue.text: Tree-hugging Eisenhower devoured Livy in translation

indicators.note: a translation renders the name in other terms, so the four letters of the Roman historian's name are rearranged

parts.note: Ike was the nickname of US president Dwight D. Eisenhower

explanation.surface: An American president wolfing down a Latin historian's text in translation, with a dash of environmentalism.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in translation' signals the anagram of the historian's name. 'devoured' only links the pieces. 'Tree-hugging' is literal: ivy clings to trunks.
explanation.definitionFit: Ivy climbs and clings around trunks, so something resembling that plant could be said to be tree-hugging.

clue.text: Artist's very excited about knight on horse

indicators.note: about here means surrounding, so the word for excited wraps the knight

parts.note: agog means eagerly excited
N is the chess notation for a knight
H is slang for heroin, known as horse

explanation.surface: A painter thrilled by the sight of a mounted knight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' puts N inside AGOG. 'on' simply places the horse's H after the rest in this down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: Vincent van Gogh was the Dutch Post-Impressionist painter of the theme's Sunflowers.

clue.text: Deceitful salesman evades answering

indicators.note: evades means the salesman gets away, so his word is removed from the longer word

parts.note: replying means answering
a rep is a sales representative

explanation.surface: A dishonest salesman dodging questions.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone telling untruths is deceitful, an adjective matching the participle used as one.

clue.text: Top man secures first place for author

indicators.note: secures here means holds within, so the monarch's word encloses the other pieces

parts.note: a king is the top man of a realm
I is the Roman numeral one, hence first
PL is the abbreviation for place, as in street names

explanation.surface: A boss making sure of first position for a writer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'secures' puts IPL inside KING.
explanation.definitionFit: Rudyard Kipling was the English writer of The Jungle Book and Kim.

clue.text: Is his art misanthropic, as some maintain?

definitions.text: Is his art misanthropic, as some maintain?

indicators.note: maintain means hold, so the run of words holds the painter's name within it

explanation.surface: A critic asks whether a painter's work shows contempt for humanity, as some claim.
explanation.walkthrough: 'maintain' doubles as 'claim' in the surface; the name sits across 'misanthropic, as some'. The whole clue also describes the painter, whose distorted figures some find cold.
explanation.definitionFit: Pablo Picasso's fractured portraits have been called hostile to humankind, which the question raises.

clue.text: See 7
17's line suggesting tours in Abbey should be organised

parts.note: the line's own opening words are not in the clue: the line merely suggests them, as the anagram signal its remaining words obey

indicators.note: should be organised says these three words are to be put in a new order, which the line itself signals with its word terrible

explanation.surface: A poet's line recommending that visits to a theatre be arranged.
explanation.walkthrough: The Abbey is Dublin's national theatre, co-founded by Yeats. The line's own opening, 'a terrible', works as an anagram signal: the three words after it rearrange 'tours in Abbey', so the line describes the clue.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the refrain of Yeats's poem Easter, 1916, so it is a line by the poet at 17.

clue.text: Pet's small (very small) and game

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for small, as on clothing labels
wee is Scottish for very small
a tie is a match, as in a cup tie

explanation.surface: Someone describes their pet as tiny and plucky.
explanation.walkthrough: 'game' looks like an adjective meaning willing, but it is a fixture: a cup tie.
explanation.definitionFit: Pet and sweetie are both terms of endearment for a loved one.

clue.text: Fanatic jousts with Conservatives over singular work by 4

indicators.note: in a down entry, the singular letter sits above the party members, placed over them
fanatic suggests wild, unrestrained, so the letters run riot into a new order

parts.note: S is the grammatical abbreviation for singular
Tories are members of the UK Conservative Party

explanation.surface: A zealot tilting at Tory politicians over a single issue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fanatic' is the anagram signal, working on 'jousts' alone; 'over' sets the singular letter above the party members in this down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: Just So Stories is Rudyard Kipling's children's book, so it is a work by the author at 4.

clue.text: Opponent fit to tackle the Greens?

definitions.meaning: ready to take on the environmental party, that is against them in attitude

explanation.surface: An adversary in good shape to take on the Green Party.
explanation.definitionFit: A person who is against something is an opponent, and an against stance suits taking on rivals.

clue.text: Carpenter's gadget pinhead left in chimney angle

parts.note: the head of a pin is its first letter, P
lum is a Scottish and northern word for a chimney

indicators.note: in means the side letter sits inside the word for a sloped edge

parts.note: a bevel is a sloping edge, an angle cut on wood

explanation.surface: A woodworker's tool: a pin's head left in the corner of a fireplace.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pinhead' is one printed word but supplies its own first letter. 'in' puts L inside BEVEL.
explanation.definitionFit: A plumb level is a tool combining a plumb line and spirit level, used by builders and joiners to check true.

clue.text: Medic with sick girl runs off to find 4's child

parts.note: MO is a medical officer

indicators.note: sick means unwell, out of sorts, so the letters are disordered
off means taken away, so the run's letter leaves the word

parts.note: R is the cricket abbreviation for runs

explanation.surface: A doctor accompanying a poorly girl rushes away to locate a writer's child.
explanation.walkthrough: 'runs off' removes R from GIRL, and 'sick' rearranges the remaining GIL into GLI.
explanation.definitionFit: Mowgli is the boy raised by wolves in Kipling's Jungle Book, so a child created by the author at 4.

clue.text: Paintings are picked up in gallery compound

indicators.note: in means these pieces are placed within the gallery's name

parts.note: the Tate is the famous London art gallery
art means paintings collectively

indicators.note: picked up means heard, so the word are is replaced by the letter it sounds like

parts.note: said aloud, these words sound like R

explanation.surface: Pictures are collected at an art museum.
explanation.walkthrough: 'picked up' turns 'are' into R; 'in' puts ARTR inside TATE.
explanation.definitionFit: A tartrate is a salt or ester of tartaric acid, a chemical compound.

clue.text: He got pit renewed to accommodate Barnum's first circus

indicators.note: to accommodate means to house, so the shuffled letters hold the showman's initial
renewed means made anew, so the letters are remade in a different order
first here means the opening letter of the showman's name

explanation.surface: A man renovating a quarry to house a famous showman's circus.
explanation.walkthrough: 'renewed' rearranges HEGOTPIT into THEIGTOP; 'to accommodate' takes in B. P. T. Barnum was the American circus impresario.
explanation.definitionFit: The big top is the main tent of a travelling show, and so stands for the circus itself.

clue.text: Batsman's opening, wholly in control of fine stroke

indicators.note: the opening of a word is its first letter
in control of means holding, so the word for wholly holds the letter for fine

parts.note: utterly means wholly
F is the abbreviation for fine, as on pencils

explanation.surface: A cricketer's opening shot played with complete command.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Batsman's opening' and 'fine stroke' suggest a cricket shot, but the stroke is in swimming.
explanation.definitionFit: Butterfly is a swimming stroke with both arms moving together over the water.

clue.text: Where various leaders of British Empire are buried? Yes

definitions.text: Where various leaders of British Empire are buried? Yes

indicators.note: various means differing, so the letters come in an altered order
the leaders of words are their initial letters

explanation.surface: Asks whether famous figures of the Empire lie in a great church, and answers itself.
explanation.walkthrough: The initials of 'British Empire are buried Yes' are rearranged. Westminster Abbey holds the tombs of monarchs and statesmen.
explanation.definitionFit: Westminster Abbey is the London church where many British kings, queens and notables are entombed.

clue.text: Guy turned to welcome English poet

indicators.note: to welcome means to take in, so the reversed rope word receives the letter
turned means turned round, read in the opposite direction

parts.note: a guy is a rope used to steady a tent or mast, also called a stay

explanation.surface: A man turning round to greet an English poet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Guy' looks like a man but is a rope, a stay; 'turned' gives YATS, and 'to welcome' puts E inside.
explanation.definitionFit: W. B. Yeats was the Irish poet who won the Nobel Prize for Literature in 1923.

clue.text: Parisian art model entertains high-class champion

parts.note: in French, tu es means thou art, so es is art to a Parisian

indicators.note: entertains means hosts, so the word for model holds the class letter

parts.note: to pose is to model for an artist
U means upper-class, as in the U and non-U distinction

explanation.surface: A model in Paris hosts a posh champion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'art' looks like painting but is the old verb form, as in 'thou art'.
explanation.definitionFit: To espouse a cause is to champion or support it, both verbs.

clue.text: Rod and his bird start to protest: "Drop your gun!"

parts.note: a stick is a rod
the emu is a large flightless Australian bird

indicators.note: the start to a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: A man called Rod and his bird begin to object at gunpoint.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rod' looks like a man's name but means a stick.
explanation.definitionFit: A robber's command for hands to go up is at odds with the instruction to drop a weapon, but both are holdup shouts.

clue.text: Former measures cramp society painters

indicators.note: cramp means confine, so the old measures squeeze the letter between them

parts.note: cubits were ancient measures of length, based on the forearm

explanation.surface: Old-fashioned restrictions hem in high-society artists.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cramp' puts S inside CUBITS.
explanation.definitionFit: Cubists such as Picasso and Braque were artists of the early twentieth-century movement.

clue.text: Fierce Unionist called to lash Tory leader

indicators.note: to lash means to bind round, so the word for called is tied around the initial

parts.note: named means called

indicators.note: the leader of a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: A fiery Unionist calls for the Conservative chief to be flogged.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lash' looks like whipping but means tie: NAMED is wrapped around T.
explanation.definitionFit: Something wild and not domesticated is ferocious, a sense close to fierce.

clue.text: Trying to hurry occasionally creates hardship

indicators.note: occasionally means now and then, so only every other letter of these words is taken

explanation.surface: Rushing about now and then makes life hard.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Trying' looks like the definition, but the definition is 'hardship'.
explanation.definitionFit: Rigour can mean harsh, severe conditions, as in the rigours of winter, which is hardship.

clue.text: Second mole crosses ebbing river faster

indicators.note: crosses means spans, so the harbour wall spans the river's reversed letters

parts.note: a mole is a breakwater or pier

indicators.note: ebbing means flowing back, so the river's name is read backwards

parts.note: the Dee is a river in Scotland and another in England and Wales

explanation.surface: A burrowing animal crossing a receding river at greater speed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mole' looks like the animal but is a harbour pier; 'ebbing' turns DEE into EED.
explanation.definitionFit: Speedier is the comparative of speedy, meaning quicker.

clue.text: See 7
Shrink from head office infiltrates a branch

indicators.note: infiltrates means gets inside, so the head office letters enter the outer pieces

parts.note: BR is the abbreviation for branch

explanation.surface: Head office staff move in on a local branch, which recoils.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shrink' looks like a psychiatrist but means recoil.
explanation.definitionFit: To loathe something is to shrink from it in disgust, and abhorrence is that recoil.

clue.text: Star declines to hug female occupants of bed

indicators.note: to hug means to hold close, so the two words clasp the female letter between them

parts.note: the Sun is our star
lowers means declines, drops

explanation.surface: A celebrity refuses to embrace the women sharing a bed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bed' looks like a sleeping place but is a flowerbed.
explanation.definitionFit: Tall yellow blooms grow in garden beds, so they are its occupants; also the title of Van Gogh's paintings.

clue.text: Take the end of August off to beat depression

indicators.note: take, paired with off, means remove the letter from the word for beat
off completes the instruction to take away a letter

parts.note: to thump is to beat

indicators.note: the end of a word is its last letter

explanation.surface: Taking a late-August holiday to fight the blues.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Take ... off' removes T, the end of August, from THUMP.
explanation.definitionFit: Having the hump is British slang for being sulky or low, so it is a fit of depression.

clue.text: Timeless web ringing Yankee city

indicators.note: ringing means encircling, so the reduced word surrounds the letter
timeless means without time, so the letter standing for time is dropped

parts.note: a network is a web
Yankee is Y in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: An everlasting web encircling an American city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Timeless' removes T (time) from NETWORK, leaving NEWORK; 'ringing' takes in Y.
explanation.definitionFit: New York is the largest city in the United States, home of the Yankees.

clue.text: Riding apace

definitions.meaning: sitting with a leg on each side, as on a horse
read as two words, a pace, one step of walking

explanation.definitionFit: A rider sits with legs either side of the saddle; a pace is a single step, or a stride.
